definition: Enthrall means to hold spellbound; to charm completely.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word enthrall. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know enthrall should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The serialized mystery enthralled the whole town; the librarian kept a waiting list forty names long for each new installment.
Interest opens the door — an interested reader keeps going, but nothing yet grips her; it stops well short of enthrall.
Obsess goes further than enthrall — an enthralled reader forgets the time; an obsessed one forgets everything else.

To mesmerize is to hold someone as if hypnotized — a trance-still, stare-fixed grip, named for the hypnotist Mesmer. Enthrall shares the captive attention but adds delight and animation: an enthralled audience laughs and leans in, while a mesmerized one sits frozen, eyes locked.

To rivet is to lock attention in place, pleasant or not — a horror film or a car crash can rivet you. Enthrall implies the grip is delightful: what enthralls holds you happily captive, so you forget the time rather than wish you could look away.
to let the attention slip loose and wander off
to wear interest down until nothing holds it
The old word still works on its own: the biography says the young poet spent two whole years in thrall to Byron.
Enthrall means to hold spellbound; to charm completely.

The new aquarium's octopus enthralls visitors so completely that the staff posts closing-time warnings at its tank alone: people miss ferries watching it unscrew jar lids and pour itself through a gap the width of a coin.
Enthrall began as a word for slavery: a thrall was a captive, and to enthrall was to enslave.
The chains have gone figurative — what enthralls you today holds your attention captive, so pleasantly that you forget to check the time.
Enthrall for delight that holds attention captive — audiences, readers, children at a tide pool.
Mesmerize when the holding feels hypnotic, rivet when it may not be pleasant at all.
Its unit-mate enamor points at the heart instead: an enthralled visitor cannot look away; an enamored one comes back tomorrow in love.

The planetarium's new operator, Mr.
Okafor, had been warned that the Tuesday school groups were the rowdiest in the county.
For the first five minutes they lived up to it, trading whispers and paper pellets under the darkened dome.
Then he dimmed the last house light, set the projector spinning toward Saturn, and began narrating the rings as if gossiping about old friends.
The show enthralled them so completely that when the lights rose, half the class groaned and asked to see it again from the start.
Their teacher checked her watch twice; forty minutes had passed, and not one student had asked to leave early.
